alt: On the left, unity: sentences link to one controlling claim while an off-topic sentence floats free. On the right, coherence: sentences S1 to S4 are chained so each leads to the next. A table gives the three levels of coherence: sentence, paragraph and text.
caption: Unity keeps every sentence on one claim; coherence links each idea to the next at every level.

alt: Three sentences about the bypass, each split into a known part and a new part, with arrows showing that the new part of one sentence becomes the known start of the next: the town built a bypass; the bypass diverted traffic; without the traffic, the shops attracted walkers.
caption: Begin with something already mentioned; end with something new.

alt: Six problems with their repairs: cut or move an off-topic sentence; add the missing idea or a transition for a jump; reorder when a conclusion precedes its evidence; keep one key term instead of shifting vocabulary; name the noun for a vague pronoun; split a paragraph with two main ideas.
caption: Most failures of unity and coherence are fixed by cutting, reordering, naming or splitting.

after: ## Weak and strong versions side by side
alt: The weak paragraph is five separate chips about bicycles, the bypass, weekend cycling, cost and helmets. The strong paragraph is four linked sentences: a controlling claim that a cycle lane would cheaply reduce traffic, then cost, then the effect on journeys, then the effect on traffic and the bypass.
caption: A controlling claim and known-then-new links turn related facts into an argument.

after: ## Worked example 1: revising a paragraph for unity and coherence
alt: Five sentences from the canteen draft tested against the controlling idea: lunch times and food-safety rules are cut, cheaper meals and more choice are kept, and packed lunches are kept only if linked to poor choice. The revision orders problem, benefit and cost.
caption: Test every sentence against the controlling idea; cut, keep or link.

after: ## Worked example 2: how coherence works in a published passage
alt: Paine’s opening moves from the crisis, to the test of character, to the reward. Two word chains run through it: difficulty (times, crisis, stands it, conflict) and reward (glorious, triumph), joined by the parallel “the harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph”.
caption: Crisis, test, reward: linked by “but”, “yet” and two chains of related words.
